claim: Type III Secretion Systems (T3SS) deliver subunits from the bacterial cytosol to nascent cell surface flagella.
source: Type III Secretion Systems (T3SS) deliver subunits from the bacterial cytosol to nascent cell surface flagella.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about T3SS function supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Early flagellar subunits that form the rod and hook substructures are unchaperoned and contain their own export signals.
source: Early flagellar subunits that form the rod and hook substructures are unchaperoned and contain their own export signals.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript and prior knowledge.

claim: A gate recognition motif (GRM) docks early flagellar subunits at the FlhBc component of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate.
source: A gate recognition motif (GRM) docks them at the FlhBc component of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript (Evans et al., 2013).

claim: The extreme N-terminus of flagellar rod and hook subunits contains a hydrophobic export signal.
source: Here, we identify a second signal at the extreme N-terminus of flagellar rod and hook subunits and determine that key to the signal is its hydrophobicity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by experimental data including deletion analysis and suppressor screens.

claim: The hydrophobicity of the N-terminal signal is key to its function.
source: Here, we identify a second signal at the extreme N-terminus of flagellar rod and hook subunits and determine that key to the signal is its hydrophobicity.
evidence: This is supported by suppressor mutation analysis showing that small non-polar residues restore function.

claim: The two export signal elements (N-terminal signal and GRM) are recognised separately and sequentially.
source: We show that the two export signal elements are recognised separately and sequentially, as the N-terminal signal is recognised by the flagellar export machinery only after subunits have docked at FlhBC via the GRM.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that FlgD∆2-5 stalls at the export machinery and blocks export, while FlgD∆2-5∆GRM does not.

claim: The N-terminal signal is recognised by the flagellar export machinery only after subunits have docked at FlhBC via the GRM.
source: We show that the two export signal elements are recognised separately and sequentially, as the N-terminal signal is recognised by the flagellar export machinery only after subunits have docked at FlhBC via the GRM.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that deletion of both signals relieves the export block caused by deletion of the N-terminal signal alone.

claim: The position of the N-terminal hydrophobic signal in the subunit sequence relative to the GRM is important for export.
source: The position of the N-terminal hydrophobic signal in the subunit sequence relative to the GRM appeared to be important
evidence: This is supported by experiments with FlgDshort and variants with different spacer lengths between the signals.

claim: FlgDshort, in which the distance between the N-terminal signal and the GRM was shortened, 'stalled' at the export machinery and was not exported.
source: a FlgD deletion variant (FlgDshort), in which the distance between the N-terminal signal and the GRM was shortened, 'stalled' at the export machinery and was not exported.
evidence: This is supported by export assays and motility assays showing reduced export and motility for FlgDshort.

claim: The attenuation of motility caused by FlgDshort was suppressed by mutations that destabilised the closed conformation of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate.
source: The attenuation of motility caused by FlgDshort was suppressed by mutations that destabilised the closed conformation of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that the FliP-M210A mutation partially suppresses the FlgDshort motility defect.

claim: The hydrophobic N-terminal signal might trigger opening of the flagellar export gate.
source: suggesting that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal might trigger opening of the flagellar export gate.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the observation that gate-opening mutations suppress FlgDshort defects.

claim: The flagellar T3SS directs the export of thousands of structural subunits required for the assembly and operation of flagella.
source: The flagellar T3SS (fT3SS) directs the export of thousands of structural subunits required for the assembly and operation of flagella, rotary nanomotors for cell motility that extend from the bacterial cell surface (Evans et al., 2014a; Evans et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellar assembly supported by citations.

claim: Newly synthesised subunits of the flagellar rod, hook and filament are unfolded and translocated across the cell membrane, powered by the protonmotive force and ATP hydrolysis.
source: Newly synthesised subunits of the flagellar rod, hook and filament are targeted to the fT3SS, where they are unfolded and translocated across the cell membrane, powered by the protonmotive force and ATP hydrolysis, into an external export channel that spans the length of the nascent flagellum (Minamino and Namba, 2008; Paul et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During flagellum biogenesis, when the rod/hook structure reaches its mature length, the fT3SS switches export specificity from recognition of 'early' rod/hook subunits to 'late' subunits for filament assembly.
source: During flagellum biogenesis, when the rod/hook structure reaches its mature length, the fT3SS switches export specificity from recognition of 'early' rod/hook subunits to 'late' subunits for filament assembly (Williams et al., 1996; Fraser et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: T3SS substrates contain N-terminal signals for targeting to the export machinery, however they do not share a common peptide sequence.
source: T3SS substrates contain N-terminal signals for targeting to the export machinery, however they do not share a common peptide sequence (Kuwajima et al., 1989; Minamino and Macnab, 1999; Kornacker and Newton, 1994; Evans et al., 2013; Végh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some T3SS substrates are piloted to the T3SS machinery by specific chaperones.
source: In addition, some substrates are piloted to the T3SS machinery by specific chaperones (Wattiau et al., 1994; Fraser et al., 1999; Thomas et al., 2004; Akeda and Galán, 2005; Bange et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The core export components of the fT3SS are evolutionarily related to those of the virulence injectisome, with which they share considerable structural and amino acid sequence similarity.
source: The core export components of the fT3SS are evolutionarily related to those of the virulence injectisome, with which they share considerable structural and amino acid sequence similarity (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Abrusci et al., 2012; Eichelberg et al., 1994; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The flagellar export machinery comprises an ATPase complex (FliHIJ) located in the cytoplasm, peripheral to the membrane.
source: The flagellar export machinery comprises an ATPase complex (FliHIJ) located in the cytoplasm, peripheral to the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of the flagellar export machinery.

claim: A nonameric ring formed by the cytoplasmic domain of FlhA (FlhAC) functions as a subunit docking platform.
source: Immediately above the ATPase is a nonameric ring formed by the cytoplasmic domain of FlhA (FlhAC), which functions as a subunit docking platform (Bange et al., 2010; Kinoshita et al., 2013; Bryant et al., 2021; Xing et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FlhA family proteins have a sea-horse-like structure, in which FlhAc forms the 'body' and the FlhA N-terminal region (FlhAN) forms the 'head', which is fixed in the plane of the membrane.
source: A recent cryo-ET map indicates that the FlhA family have a sea-horse-like structure, in which FlhAc forms the 'body' and the FlhA N-terminal region (FlhAN) forms the 'head', which is fixed in the plane of the membrane (Butan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cryo-ET structural data cited from Butan et al., 2019.

claim: FlhAN wraps around the base of a complex formed by FliPQR and the N-terminal sub-domain of FlhB (FlhBN), and together these form the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate.
source: FlhAN wraps around the base of a complex formed by FliPQR and the N-terminal sub-domain of FlhB (FlhBN), and together these form the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate that connects the cytoplasm to the central channel in the nascent flagellum, which is contiguous with the extracellular environment (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Abrusci et al., 2012; Eichelberg et al., 1994; Johnson et al., 2019; Bryant et al., 2021; Xing et al., 2018; Butan et al., 2019; Mizuno et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple structural studies.

claim: FlhBC functions as a docking site for early flagellar subunits.
source: FlhBN is connected via a linker (FlhBCN) to the cytoplasmic domain of FlhB (FlhBC), which is thought to sit between the FlhAN and FlhAC rings, where it functions as a docking site for early flagellar subunits (Evans et al., 2013; Kuhlen et al., 2018; Butan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The gate recognition motif (GRM) is a small hydrophobic sequence that is essential for early subunit export.
source: We have shown that of one of these signals is a small hydrophobic sequence termed the gate recognition motif (GRM), which is essential for early subunit export (Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors cited as Evans et al., 2013.

claim: The GRM binds a surface exposed hydrophobic pocket on FlhBc.
source: This motif binds a surface exposed hydrophobic pocket on FlhBc (Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited as Evans et al., 2013.

claim: Subunits must be unfolded before they can pass through the narrow channel formed by FliPQR-FlhBN into the central channel of the nascent flagellum.
source: Once subunits reach the export machinery, they must be unfolded before they can pass through the narrow channel formed by FliPQR-FlhBN into the central channel of the nascent flagellum, through which the subunits transit until they reach the tip and fold into the structure (Evans et al., 2014b; Kuhlen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FliPQR-FlhBN adopts an energetically favourable closed conformation to maintain the membrane permeability barrier.
source: Structural studies suggest that FliPQR-FlhBN adopts an energetically favourable closed conformation, possibly to maintain the membrane permeability barrier (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2018; Kuhlen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: There must be a mechanism to trigger opening of the export gate when subunits dock at cytosolic face of the flagellar export machinery.
source: This suggests that there must be a mechanism to trigger opening of the export gate when subunits dock at cytosolic face of the flagellar export machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the gate is normally closed but must open for export.

claim: Loss of FlgD residues 2–5 caused a significant reduction in export.
source: Loss of residues 2–5 caused a significant reduction in export, as did deletion of residues 36–40, although to a lesser extent (Figure 1A; Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Deletion of FlgD residues 36–40 caused a reduction in export, although to a lesser extent than deletion of residues 2-5.
source: Loss of residues 2–5 caused a significant reduction in export, as did deletion of residues 36–40, although to a lesser extent (Figure 1A; Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FlgD residues 36–40 are the gate recognition motif (GRM) required for transient subunit docking at the FlhBC component of the export gate.
source: We have shown that FlgD residues 36–40 are the gate recognition motif (GRM) required for transient subunit docking at the FlhBC component of the export gate (Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited as Evans et al., 2013.

claim: All intragenic suppressor mutations within amino acids 1–40 of FlgD isolated from the FlgDΔ2–5 variant were located between the gate-recognition motif (GRM) and the extreme N-terminus.
source: All suppressor mutations were located between the gate-recognition motif (GRM, blue) and the extreme N-terminus, and can be separated into two classes: insertions or duplications that introduced additional sequence between valine-15 and the gate-recognition motif, or missense mutations that re-introduce small non-polar residues at the N-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and schematic shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Suppressor mutations from FlgDΔ2–5 can be separated into two classes: insertions or duplications that introduced additional sequence between valine-15 and the gate-recognition motif, or missense mutations that re-introduce small non-polar residues at the N-terminus.
source: All suppressor mutations were located between the gate-recognition motif (GRM, blue) and the extreme N-terminus, and can be separated into two classes: insertions or duplications that introduced additional sequence between valine-15 and the gate-recognition motif, or missense mutations that re-introduce small non-polar residues at the N-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and schematic shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Missense mutations in FlgDΔ2–5 suppressors introduced small non-polar residues at the extreme N-terminus of FlgD∆2–5.
source: The first class of motile revertants carried flgD∆2–5 alleles with missense mutations that introduced small non-polar residues at the extreme N-terminus of FlgD∆2–5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of residues 2–5 (2SIAV5) removed all small non-polar amino acids from the first ten residue region of FlgD.
source: Deletion of residues 2–5 (2SIAV5) had removed all small non-polar amino acids from the first ten residue region of FlgD, effectively creating a new N-terminus containing a combination of polar, charged or large non-polar residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All flagellar rod and hook subunit N-terminal regions contain small non-polar residues positioned upstream of the gate recognition motif (GRM).
source: Analysis of other flagellar rod and hook subunit primary sequences revealed that in every case their native N-terminal regions contain small non-polar residues positioned upstream of the gate recognition motif (GRM residues 36–40; Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hydrophobicity is key to the function of the N-terminal export signal.
source: indicating that hydrophobicity may be key to the function of the N-terminal export signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all rod/hook subunits have small non-polar residues near the N-terminus.

claim: Removal of non-polar residues from the extreme N-terminus of FliK attenuated its export.
source: Removal of non-polar residues from the extreme N-terminus of the secreted hook-length control protein, FliK, attenuated its export, indicating that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal is required for export of early subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The hydrophobic N-terminal signal is required for export of early subunits.
source: Removal of non-polar residues from the extreme N-terminus of the secreted hook-length control protein, FliK, attenuated its export, indicating that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal is required for export of early subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the FliK deletion experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Export of FlgD∆2–5-N8I and FlgD∆2–5-T11I recovered to ~50% of the level observed for wild type FlgD.
source: Export assays performed with two representative motile revertant strains carrying flgD∆2–5 variants with gain-of-function point mutations, those encoding FlgD∆2–5-N8I and FlgD∆2–5-T11I, revealed that export of these subunits had recovered to ~50% of the level observed for wild type FlgD (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplements 4–5).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: Both FlgD∆2-5-19AGAGAG20 and FlgD∆2-5-19STSTST20 were exported as effectively as the gain-of-function mutant FlgD∆2-5-19GSGSMT20.
source: We found that both the engineered FlgD variants (FlgD∆2-5-19AGAGAG20 and FlgD∆2-5-19STSTST20) were exported from a Salmonella flgD null strain as effectively as the gain-of-function mutant FlgD∆2-5-19GSGSMT20 isolated from the suppressor screen (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The insertions in FlgD∆2–5 suppressors repositioned a sequence in the FlgD∆2–5 N-terminus relative to the GRM to overcome the loss of small hydrophobic residues.
source: This suggests that the insertions had repositioned a sequence in the FlgD∆2–5 N-terminus relative to the GRM to overcome the loss of small hydrophobic residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both polar and non-polar insertions restore export.

claim: The insertions in FlgD∆2–5 suppressors were all located between the GRM and valine15 (V15).
source: Sequence analysis of the gain-of-function FlgD∆2–5 insertion variants revealed that the insertions were all located between the GRM and valine15 (V15; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The insertions in FlgD∆2–5 suppressors repositioned valine15 relative to the GRM, such that it could perform the function of the N-terminal hydrophobic signal lost in FlgD∆2–5.
source: We reasoned that they repositioned valine15 relative to the GRM, such that it could perform the function of the N-terminal hydrophobic signal lost in FlgD∆2–5.
evidence: This is inferred from the position of insertions and tested by V15A mutation.

claim: The flgD null strain carrying variant FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A was non-motile.
source: Unlike the flgD null strain producing either the parental FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20 or wild type FlgD, the flgD null carrying variant FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A was non-motile, reflecting the variant's failure to export (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The V15 residue compensated for the missing N-terminal hydrophobic signal in FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20.
source: This suggests that the V15 residue had indeed compensated for the missing N-terminal hydrophobic signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that V15A mutation abolishes export in the suppressor background.

claim: Four gain-of-function missense mutations (M7I, D9A, T11I and G14V) were identified from screening for intragenic suppressors of FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A.
source: By screening for intragenic suppressors of the motility defect associated with FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A, four gain-of-function missense mutations were identified, M7I, D9A, T11I and G14V.
evidence: This is supported by suppressor screen data.

claim: All gain-of-function mutations from FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A introduced small hydrophobic residues positioned at least 27 residues upstream of the GRM.
source: All these had introduced small hydrophobic residues, all positioned at least 27 residues upstream of the GRM.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of suppressor mutations.

claim: FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A gain-of-function variants restored motility to the Salmonella flgD null strain and were exported at levels similar to wildtype FlgD and FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20.
source: These FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20-V15A gain-of-function variants restored motility to the Salmonella flgD null strain and were exported at levels similar to wildtype FlgD and FlgD∆2-5-19(GSGSMT)20 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In all Salmonella flagellar rod/hook subunits the GRM is positioned ≥30 amino acids downstream of the subunit N-terminus.
source: In the primary sequences of all Salmonella flagellar rod/hook subunits the GRM is positioned ≥30 amino acids downstream of the subunit N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Separation of the two export signals by a minimum number of residues is a common feature among early flagellar subunits.
source: suggesting that separation of the two signals by a minimum number of residues might be a common feature among early flagellar subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis of all rod/hook subunits.

claim: The minimum number of inserted GSTNAS repeats that could support efficient FlgD export was three, equivalent to separation of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM by 24 residues.
source: Swimming motility and export assays revealed that the minimum number of inserted GSTNAS repeats that could support efficient FlgD export was three, equivalent to separation of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM by 24 residues (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Below the threshold of 24 residues separation, FlgD export and swimming motility were strongly attenuated.
source: Below this threshold, FlgD export and swimming motility were strongly attenuated (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Motility and FlgD export increased incrementally with the addition of each amino acid between the N-terminal signal and GRM in FlgD∆9–32 variants with two GSTNAS repeats.
source: Motility and FlgD export increased incrementally with the addition of each amino acid (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A low level of FlgD export is supported when the hydrophobic N-terminal signal (2SIAV5) and the GRM (36FLTLL40) are separated by 19 residues.
source: The data indicate that a low level of FlgD export is supported when the hydrophobic N-terminal signal (2SIAV5) and the GRM (36FLTLL40) are separated by 19 residues, with export efficiency and swimming motility increasing as separation of the export signals approaches an optimal 24 residues.
evidence: This is based on the incremental addition experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Export efficiency and swimming motility increase as separation of the export signals approaches an optimal 24 residues.
source: The data indicate that a low level of FlgD export is supported when the hydrophobic N-terminal signal (2SIAV5) and the GRM (36FLTLL40) are separated by 19 residues, with export efficiency and swimming motility increasing as separation of the export signals approaches an optimal 24 residues.
evidence: This is based on the incremental addition experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Seven gain-of-function mutations from FlgDshort introduced additional residues between the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM.
source: Sequencing of flgDshort alleles from motile revertant strains identified seven gain-of-function mutations that introduced additional residues between the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: FlgDshort gain-of-function variants showed increased FlgD subunit export and swimming motility compared to FlgDshort.
source: Swimming motility and FlgD export was assessed for three flgD null strains expressing representative flgDshort gain-of-function variants and all showed increased FlgD subunit export and swimming motility compared to the flgD null expressing flgDshort (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The position of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal relative to the GRM is critical for efficient FlgD subunit export.
source: The data confirm that the position of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal relative to the GRM is critical for efficient FlgD subunit export.
evidence: This is supported by the FlgDshort suppressor data.

claim: Export of FlgEshort and FlgGshort variants was severely attenuated compared to wild-type FlgE and FlgG.
source: As had been observed for FlgDshort, export of the FlgEshort and FlgGshort variants was severely attenuated compared to wild-type FlgE and FlgG (Figure 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Insertion of four GSTNAS repeats into FlgEshort and FlgGshort recovered subunit export to wild-type levels.
source: Furthermore, insertion of four GSTNAS repeats into FlgEshort and FlgGshort recovered subunit export to wild-type levels, indicating that the minimum separation of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM is a feature throughout rod and hook subunits (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The minimum separation of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM is a feature throughout rod and hook subunits.
source: Furthermore, insertion of four GSTNAS repeats into FlgEshort and FlgGshort recovered subunit export to wild-type levels, indicating that the minimum separation of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM is a feature throughout rod and hook subunits (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experiments with FlgE and FlgG shown in Figure 3.

claim: FlgD∆2–5 inhibited motility and export of the FliK, FlgK and FlgL flagellar subunits.
source: We saw that FlgD∆2–5 inhibited motility and export of the FliK, FlgK and FlgL flagellar subunits, whereas FlgD∆GRM did not (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: FlgD∆GRM did not inhibit motility and export of FliK, FlgK and FlgL flagellar subunits.
source: We saw that FlgD∆2–5 inhibited motility and export of the FliK, FlgK and FlgL flagellar subunits, whereas FlgD∆GRM did not (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: FlgD∆2–5 enters the flagellar export pathway and stalls at a critical point, blocking export.
source: The data indicate that FlgD∆2–5 enters the flagellar export pathway and stalls at a critical point, blocking export.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FlgD∆2–5 blocks export of other subunits.

claim: FlgD∆GRM does not stall or block export.
source: In contrast, FlgD∆GRM does not stall or block export.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FlgD∆GRM does not block export of other subunits.

claim: The Salmonella ∆recA strain producing FlgD∆2–5∆GRM displayed swimming motility and levels of FliK and FlgK subunit export similar to cells producing FlgD∆GRM.
source: Motility and subunit export assays revealed that the Salmonella ∆recA strain producing FlgD∆2–5∆GRM displayed swimming motility and levels of FliK and FlgK subunit export similar to cells producing FlgD∆GRM (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: FlgD∆2–5 stalls after docking at the FlhBC export gate, preventing docking of other early subunits.
source: The data suggest that FlgD∆2–5 stalls after docking at the FlhBC export gate, preventing docking of other early subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of both signals relieves the block.

claim: FlgEshort and FlgDshort inhibited swimming motility and the export of other flagellar subunits (FliD, FliK, FlgK).
source: Compared to the wild-type subunits expressed in trans, the 'short' subunits inhibited swimming motility and the export of other flagellar subunits (FliD, FliK, FlgK), whereas FlgEshort∆GRM and FlgDshort∆GRM did not (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: FlgEshort∆GRM and FlgDshort∆GRM did not inhibit swimming motility and export of other flagellar subunits.
source: Compared to the wild-type subunits expressed in trans, the 'short' subunits inhibited swimming motility and the export of other flagellar subunits (FliD, FliK, FlgK), whereas FlgEshort∆GRM and FlgDshort∆GRM did not (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by motility and export assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The subunit GRM and the hydrophobic N-terminal signal are recognised sequentially, with subunits first docking at FlhBC via the GRM, which positions the hydrophobic N-terminal signal for subsequent interactions with the export machinery.
source: Taken together with the data presented in Figure 4, the results indicate that the subunit GRM and the hydrophobic N-terminal signal are recognised sequentially, with subunits first docking at FlhBC via the GRM, which positions the hydrophobic N-terminal signal for subsequent interactions with the export machinery (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that deletion of GRM relieves stalling caused by loss of N-terminal signal.

claim: FliPQR-FlhBN and the subunit docking site on FlhBC are separated by a minimum distance of ~78 Å.
source: The model indicated that FliPQR-FlhBN and the subunit docking site on FlhBC are separated by a minimum distance of ~78 Å, and that FlhBC is positioned no more than ~22–45 Å from FlhA (Figure 6A; Butan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: FlhBC is positioned no more than ~22–45 Å from FlhA.
source: The model indicated that FliPQR-FlhBN and the subunit docking site on FlhBC are separated by a minimum distance of ~78 Å, and that FlhBC is positioned no more than ~22–45 Å from FlhA (Figure 6A; Butan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The distance between the FlgD N-terminal hydrophobic signal and the GRM is in the range of ~45 Å (α-helix) to ~105 Å (unfolded contour length), depending on the predicted structure adopted by the subunit N-terminus.
source: Taking FlgD as a model early flagellar subunit, the distance between the FlgD N-terminal hydrophobic signal and the GRM was found to be in the range of ~45 Å (α-helix) to ~105 Å (unfolded contour length), depending on the predicted structure adopted by the subunit N-terminus (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 6A.

claim: It is feasible that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal of a subunit docked at FlhBC could contact either FlhA or the FliPQR-FlhBN complex.
source: Based on these estimates, it seemed feasible that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal of a subunit docked at FlhBC could contact either FlhA or the FliPQR-FlhBN complex, and that this interaction might trigger opening of the export gate (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Meshcheryakov et al., 2013; Bryant and Fraser, 2021; Vonderviszt et al., 1992).
evidence: This is speculative, based on distance estimates from structural modeling.

claim: The interaction of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal with the export machinery might trigger opening of the export gate.
source: Based on these estimates, it seemed feasible that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal of a subunit docked at FlhBC could contact either FlhA or the FliPQR-FlhBN complex, and that this interaction might trigger opening of the export gate (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Meshcheryakov et al., 2013; Bryant and Fraser, 2021; Vonderviszt et al., 1992).
evidence: This is speculative, based on the observation that gate-opening mutations suppress FlgDshort defects.

claim: FliP-M210A mutation increases ion conductance across the bacterial inner membrane, indicating that this gate variant fails to close efficiently.
source: One such export gate mutation, FliP-M210A, has been shown to increase ion conductance across the bacterial inner membrane, indicating that this gate variant fails to close efficiently (Kuhlen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited as Kuhlen et al., 2020.

claim: The swimming motility of the fliP-M210A-∆flgD strain expressing FlgDshort had a 50% greater diameter than that of the wild type fliP-∆flgD strain expressing FlgDshort.
source: The swimming motility of these strains was found to be consistently stronger in the strain producing the M210A gate compared to the strain with the wild-type gate, with the motility halo of the fliP-M210A-∆flgD strain expressing FlgDshort having a 50% greater diameter than that of the wild type fliP-∆flgD strain expressing FlgDshort (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The defect caused by incorrect positioning of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal relative to the GRM in FlgDshort can be partially compensated by promoting the gate open conformation.
source: This increase in motility indicated that the defect caused by incorrect positioning of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal relative to the GRM in FlgDshort could indeed be partially compensated by promoting the gate open conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FliP-M210A partially suppresses FlgDshort defects.

claim: Loss of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal in FlgD had a stronger negative effect on subunit export than deletion of the GRM.
source: Loss of the hydrophobic N-terminal signal in the hook cap subunit FlgD had a stronger negative effect on subunit export than deletion of the GRM that enables subunit docking at FlhBC
evidence: This is supported by the export assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The hydrophobic N-terminal signal may be required to trigger an essential export step.
source: suggesting that the hydrophobic N-terminal signal may be required to trigger an essential export step.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the observation that loss of the N-terminal signal has a strong effect on export.

claim: All early subunits contain small hydrophobic residues close to the N-terminus.
source: All early subunits contain small hydrophobic residues close to the N-terminus, but FlgD is unique in that only four (I3, A4, V5 and V15) of its first 25 residues are small and non-polar (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: FlgD is unique in that only four (I3, A4, V5 and V15) of its first 25 residues are small and non-polar.
source: All early subunits contain small hydrophobic residues close to the N-terminus, but FlgD is unique in that only four (I3, A4, V5 and V15) of its first 25 residues are small and non-polar (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of residues 2–5 in FlgD removes the critical hydrophobic N-terminal signal.
source: While deletion of residues 2–5 in FlgD removes the critical hydrophobic N-terminal signal, similar deletions in the N-terminal regions of other rod/hook subunits reposition existing small non-polar residues close to the N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Similar deletions in the N-terminal regions of other rod/hook subunits reposition existing small non-polar residues close to the N-terminus.
source: While deletion of residues 2–5 in FlgD removes the critical hydrophobic N-terminal signal, similar deletions in the N-terminal regions of other rod/hook subunits reposition existing small non-polar residues close to the N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Previous deletion studies in early flagellar subunits have failed to identify the hydrophobic N-terminal signal because similar deletions in other subunits reposition existing small non-polar residues.
source: This is perhaps why previous deletion studies in early flagellar subunits have failed to identify the hydrophobic N-terminal signal (Evans et al., 2013; Hirano et al., 2005; Minamino et al., 1999).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the unique properties of FlgD.

claim: A FlgN chaperone variant lacking the C-terminal 20 residues stalls at the FliI ATPase.
source: For example, a FlgN chaperone variant lacking the C-terminal 20 residues stalls at the FliI ATPase (Thomas et al., 2004)
evidence: This is based on prior work cited as Thomas et al., 2004.

claim: A GST-tagged FliJ binds FlhA but is unable to associate correctly with FliI so blocking wild type FliJ interaction with FlhA.
source: while a GST-tagged FliJ binds FlhA but is unable to associate correctly with FliI so blocking wild type FliJ interaction with FlhA (Ibuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited as Ibuki et al., 2012.

claim: The N-terminal region of flagellar subunits is often unstructured in solution.
source: The N-terminal region of flagellar subunits is often unstructured in solution (Kuwajima et al., 1989; Minamino and Macnab, 1999; Kornacker and Newton, 1994; Evans et al., 2013; Végh et al., 2006; Vonderviszt et al., 1992)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Disorder in the N-terminal region may be an intrinsic feature of flagellar export signals.
source: and such disorder may be an intrinsic feature of flagellar export signals (Kuwajima et al., 1989; Minamino and Macnab, 1999; Kornacker and Newton, 1994; Evans et al., 2013; Végh et al., 2006; Weber-Sparenberg et al., 2006; Aizawa et al., 1990)
evidence: This is speculative, based on observations of disorder in export signals.

claim: Unstructured signals are typical in other bacterial export N-terminal substrate signals such as those of the Sec and Tat systems.
source: as they are typical in other bacterial export N-terminal substrate signals such as those of the Sec and Tat systems (Tsirigotaki et al., 2017; Palmer and Berks, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Unstructured signals may facilitate multiple interactions with different binding partners during export.
source: Unstructured signals may facilitate multiple interactions with different binding partners during export, and in the case of export systems that transport unfolded proteins they may aid initial entry of substrates into narrow export channels (Tsirigotaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by a citation.

claim: Signal peptides in TAT pathway substrates switch between disordered and α-helical conformations depending on the hydrophobicity of the environment.
source: Signal peptides in TAT pathway substrates switch between disordered and α-helical conformations depending on the hydrophobicity of the environment (San Miguel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Local environments along the flagellar export pathway will likely influence the conformation of subunit export signals.
source: It therefore seems likely that local environments along the flagellar export pathway will influence the conformation of subunit export signals (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Erhardt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on observations in other systems.

claim: FlgD variants that contain additional sequence that position the N-terminal export signal and GRM further apart far above the required threshold did not impede export.
source: Interestingly, FlgD variants that contain additional sequence that position the N-terminal export signal and GRM further apart far above the required threshold did not impede export, which argues that the sequence between both export signals is unfolded (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on export assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: The sequence between the N-terminal export signal and GRM is unfolded.
source: Interestingly, FlgD variants that contain additional sequence that position the N-terminal export signal and GRM further apart far above the required threshold did not impede export, which argues that the sequence between both export signals is unfolded (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that extra sequence does not impede export.

claim: If the region between the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM is unstructured and extended, this would correspond to a polypeptide contour length of approximately 72–105 Å.
source: If the region between the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM is unstructured and extended, this would correspond to a polypeptide contour length of approximately 72–105 Å (where the length of one amino acid is ~3.6 Å).
evidence: This is a calculation based on standard polypeptide dimensions.

claim: If the region between the hydrophobic N-terminal signal and the GRM were to fold as an α-helix, its length would be approximately 30–36 Å.
source: If the same region were to fold as an α-helix, its length would be approximately 30–36 Å (where one amino acid rises every ~1.5 Å).
evidence: This is a calculation based on standard α-helix dimensions.

claim: Placement of the AlphaFold predicted structure of full length FlhB into a tomogram of the T3SS suggests that FlhBC is positioned below the plane of the inner membrane but above the nonameric ring of FlhAC.
source: Placement of the AlphaFold predicted structure of full length FlhB into a tomogram of the T3SS suggests that FlhBC is positioned below the plane of the inner membrane but above the nonameric ring of FlhAC (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: One function of the subunit hydrophobic N-terminal signal might be to trigger opening of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate.
source: We speculate that one function of the subunit hydrophobic N-terminal signal might be to trigger opening of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate, which rests in an energetically favourable closed conformation to maintain the permeability barrier across the bacterial inner membrane (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Butan et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2018; Kuhlen et al., 2020; Bryant and Fraser, 2021).
evidence: This is speculative, based on the observation that gate-opening mutations suppress FlgDshort defects.

claim: The FlhAB-FliPQR export gate rests in an energetically favourable closed conformation to maintain the permeability barrier across the bacterial inner membrane.
source: We speculate that one function of the subunit hydrophobic N-terminal signal might be to trigger opening of the FlhAB-FliPQR export gate, which rests in an energetically favourable closed conformation to maintain the permeability barrier across the bacterial inner membrane (Kuhlen et al., 2018; Butan et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2018; Kuhlen et al., 2020; Bryant and Fraser, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FliPQR contains three gating regions: the R-plug, M-gasket, and Q-latch.
source: The atomic resolution structure of FliPQR showed that it contains three gating regions (Kuhlen et al., 2018). FliR provides a loop (the R-plug) that sits within the core of the structure. Below this, five copies of FliP each provides three methionine residues that together form a methionine-rich ring (M-gasket) under which ionic interactions between adjacent FliQ subunits hold the base of the structure shut (Q-latch).
evidence: This is based on structural data cited as Kuhlen et al., 2018.

claim: The R-plug, M-gasket, and Q-latch stabilize the closed export gate conformation to maintain the membrane barrier.
source: Mutational and evolutionary analyses have shown that the R-plug, M-gasket, and Q-latch stabilize the closed export gate conformation to maintain the membrane barrier, preventing the leakage of small molecules whilst allowing the passage of substrates into the export channel (Bryant and Fraser, 2021; Hüsing et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The FliPQR export gate opens and closes in response to export substrate availability.
source: We have also shown that the FliPQR export gate opens and closes in response to export substrate availability, indicating that the export gate reverts to a closed conformation in the absence of export substrates, thereby maintaining the integrity of the cell membrane (Bryant and Fraser, 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors cited as Bryant and Fraser, 2021.

claim: The export gate must be opened in response to substrate docking at the export machinery.
source: These data indicate that the export gate must be opened in response to substrate docking at the export machinery (Bryant and Fraser, 2021; Hüsing et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from observations about gate dynamics.

claim: The surface-exposed hydrophobic GRM-binding pocket on FlhBC is well conserved across the T3SS SctU family.
source: The surface-exposed hydrophobic GRM-binding pocket on FlhBC is well conserved across the T3SS SctU family, to which FlhB belongs (Evans et al., 2013; Zarivach et al., 2008; Lountos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The GRM is conserved in all four injectisome early subunits (SctI, SctF, SctP, OrgC) and is located at least 30 residues away from small hydrophobic residues near the subunit N-terminus.
source: Furthermore, the GRM is conserved in all four injectisome early subunits (SctI, SctF, SctP, OrgC) and is located at least 30 residues away from small hydrophobic residues near the subunit N-terminus (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The 'dual signal' mechanism proposed for early flagellar export likely operates in all T3SS pathways.
source: It therefore seems plausible that the 'dual signal' mechanism we propose for early flagellar export operates in all T3SS pathways.
evidence: This is speculative, based on conservation of the signals in injectisome subunits.

claim: In the outer membrane chitin transporter in Vibrio, the N-terminus of a neighbouring subunit acts as a pore plug in the closed conformation.
source: The outer membrane chitin transporter in Vibrio adopts a closed conformation in which the N-terminus of a neighbouring subunit acts as a pore plug (Aunkham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Chitin binding to the Vibrio chitin transporter ejects the plug, opening the transport channel and allowing chitin transport.
source: Chitin binding to the transporter ejects the plug, opening the transport channel and allowing chitin transport (Aunkham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In the Sec pathway, interactions of SecA, ribosomes or pre-proteins with SecYEG can induce conformational changes that promote channel opening.
source: In the Sec pathway, interactions of SecA, ribosomes or pre-proteins with SecYEG can induce conformational changes that promote channel opening (Tsirigotaki et al., 2017; Ge et al., 2014; Zimmer et al., 2008; Voorhees et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the TAT system, substrate binding to the TatBC complex triggers association with, and subsequent polymerisation of, TatA, which is required for substrate translocation.
source: In the TAT system, which transports folded substrates across the cytoplasmic membrane, substrate binding to the TatBC complex triggers association with, and subsequent polymerisation of, TatA, which is required for substrate translocation (Palmer and Berks, 2012; Mori and Cline, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Substrate-triggered channel opening mechanisms serve to conserve energy and prevent disruption of the membrane permeability barrier.
source: All of these mechanisms serve both to conserve energy and prevent disruption of the membrane permeability barrier.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the examples provided.

claim: The signal of non-polar residues within the N-termini of early rod/hook subunits trigger export gate opening in a manner comparable to other transport systems.
source: Our data suggest that in a comparable way the signal of non-polar residues within the N-termini of early rod/hook subunits trigger export gate opening.
evidence: This is speculative, based on analogy with other systems and the suppression data.
